title: The Fifth Violin
subtitle: An Old Workshop on Corrientes
summary: Renata is eleven and plays violin at a music school in Buenos Aires. Her teacher sends her to an old luthier's workshop on Corrientes Avenue to have a small crack repaired. Inside, she sees four identical violins hanging on the wall, made by the same maker two hundred years ago, each once belonging to a different famous player. The luthier tells her a fifth violin was made and is lost. Renata decides she is going to find it.

paragraphs: Renata was eleven, and she had been playing the violin for six years, and she was one of the better students at the small music school in the neighborhood of Almagro in Buenos Aires. Her violin was not her own — the school lent it to her — but she had been using the same one for two years, and it felt like hers. On a Thursday in the middle of March, at the end of a rehearsal, her teacher had noticed a tiny crack near the base of the neck. Not big enough to affect the sound. But if it was left alone it would get worse. Her teacher had written down an address on a card. "Don Aurelio," she had said. "On Corrientes. He is the best luthier in the city. Take it after school on Monday. He will not charge you. He does the school violins for free. Tell him I sent you."

So on Monday, in her school uniform, Renata took the subway to the Corrientes stop, and she walked along the huge busy street with her violin case in her hand. Corrientes was the great theater street of Buenos Aires — full of bookshops that stayed open until two in the morning, and old cafes, and marquees for tango shows and plays. Renata knew it well. Her parents used to bring her to the bookshops when she was small. She walked for maybe ten minutes, checking the number on the card, until she found the doorway.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior view of a narrow old staircase going up in a Buenos Aires building. Iron banister, worn stone steps, warm afternoon light through a high window. A girl (Renata, 11, uniform, violin case) climbs the stairs. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: The workshop was on the third floor of an old building. The staircase was narrow and had iron banisters, and each stone step was worn smooth in the middle from a hundred years of use. Renata climbed carefully. She was a little nervous. She had never been to a luthier before. She had imagined a workshop something like a fancy shop, but the building did not feel like a shop — it felt like an old apartment building, with the smell of cooking and the sound of someone playing a radio behind one of the doors she passed.

The door at the top said, in small careful painted letters, ATELIER AURELIO SANTOS. LUTHIER. There was no bell. Renata knocked. After a moment the door opened and a man was there. He was maybe fifty, tall, thin, with silver at his temples and dark eyes and a leather apron over his shirt. He looked at her for a moment. He said, in a quiet voice, "You must be sent by Señora Vilar. She always sends the smaller ones on Mondays. Come in."

paragraphs: The workshop was one big room. It had very high ceilings and huge old windows that let in a lot of warm afternoon light. Everything smelled of wood shavings and something else — a resinous smell that Renata could not name. There were half-finished violins hanging from hooks all around. There was a long wooden workbench along one wall with tiny brass tools laid out in careful rows. There was a small desk in one corner with paperwork on it. There was a chair for a customer. And on the far wall, in a straight line, there were four completely identical violins hanging on hooks. Renata noticed them almost immediately. She could not stop looking at them.

Don Aurelio saw her looking. He said, "Yes. Those. They are one of the reasons people come to see me. They are the reason my father bought this workshop, in fact. Come. Sit. Give me your violin. I will look at the crack. Then, if you want, we can talk about them."

Renata gave him her violin. She sat in the customer chair. She kept looking at the four violins on the wall. They were the same size. They were the same color — a warm dark amber varnish that seemed to have a small glow of its own, even in the daylight. They had the same fingerboard. The same shape. The same little curls at the ends of the scrolls. They were not just similar. They were identical. Like four copies of the same photograph.

Don Aurelio worked on Renata's violin at his bench. He barely looked at it — he had been doing this so long, she realized, that his hands knew what to do without much of him being there. He said, in his soft voice, while he worked, "They are called the Constanzi Quartet. Made by a maker named Filippo Constanzi in Cremona, Italy, in 1801. He was a student of one of the great old makers. He made these four violins as a set, at the same time, from wood from the same tree. He wanted to give them all the same voice. So a string quartet could play them, and no one violin would stand out above the others. All matched. All the same."

Renata (11) sits watching him, chin in hands. Warm ambient afternoon light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: When Don Aurelio had finished with her violin — the crack, he said, was small; he would fill it and revarnish it and she could pick it up on Friday — he stood up and went to the wall. He pointed at each of the four in turn. "This one belonged to a man named Bernardo Molina. A famous Argentine violinist. He played on it for forty years. When he died, in 1972, his widow sold it to my father. This one belonged to a Frenchwoman named Cecile Petit, who played in the Paris Opera in the 1880s. This one belonged to a Russian named Karyakin, who played in Moscow before the Revolution. He escaped Russia in 1918 with only this violin and the clothes on his back. This one — the last one — belonged to a young man named Diego Palma. He was Argentine also. He was going to be very famous. He died young. He was twenty-four."

He turned to Renata. "They came to my father one at a time. Over forty years. He tracked them down. He bought them from families, from estates. He believed — he truly believed — that they belonged together. That they had been made to be together. When my father died I promised him I would keep them together. So here they are. Four of the five. Together." Renata sat up. "Four of the five," she said. Don Aurelio smiled. "Yes," he said. "There is a fifth. There was always a fifth."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior close view. Don Aurelio has opened a very old leather-bound book on his workbench. He is pointing at a page written in old Italian. Renata (11) leans in to look. Warm afternoon light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: Don Aurelio brought out a very old leather-bound book from a shelf. He opened it. It was written in Italian. He said, "This is Constanzi's own workshop record. Each violin he made, he wrote down. Where it went. Who took it. The measurements. Everything. I have this book because my father tracked it down in Cremona in 1970. It is one of the few Constanzi workshop books that still exist." He turned to a specific page. "Look. Here. May 1801. Five violins delivered to a merchant in Genoa named Ravello. The merchant paid for all five in one payment. He was going to take them to Naples and sell them to a musical family who had commissioned them for a private quintet — one violin for each of five children."

"But the fifth," Renata said. "What happened to the fifth." Don Aurelio shook his head slowly. "That is what nobody knows. The merchant did make it to Naples. Records show he delivered five violins. But the family who received them only kept four. Nobody knows why. Maybe one child did not want to play. Maybe the fifth was damaged in transit. Maybe it was stolen along the way and replaced with something else. Whatever happened, the fifth Constanzi does not appear in any record after 1801. It vanished. My father spent thirty years looking for it. He never found it. He died in 2015 not knowing what happened to it."

Renata looked at the four on the wall. Then at Don Aurelio. "But — you said your father tracked down four of them. Wouldn't the fifth have — surfaced somewhere. It has been two hundred years." "Yes," said Don Aurelio. "That is what he thought too. That eventually it would appear at an auction, or in an old estate somewhere, and he would find it. But it never has. That is very strange. A Constanzi is a valuable violin — even a small one. If someone had it and knew what it was, they would sell it. They would insure it. Something. But there has been no trace of it in two hundred years. That means either it was destroyed — burned, lost at sea, broken — or it is somewhere where its owner does not know what it is. Where it is being used as a normal violin. That is what my father believed, at the end of his life. That somewhere, someone is playing the fifth Constanzi and does not know."

"How would you know if you saw it," said Renata. Don Aurelio thought about this. "You would know two ways. First — you would look at it. It has the exact same shape as the four on the wall. Same curls, same fingerboard, same varnish color. Constanzi signed his violins with a specific mark inside — a small C inside a small circle, painted on the label. If a violin has that mark, and it looks like these four, it is the fifth. Second — you would listen. Constanzi violins have a very particular voice. A specific tone. Even to an untrained ear, if you know what these four sound like, and you hear the fifth, you would know it was one of theirs."

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior close view. Renata (11) sits still on the customer chair, thinking hard. Her face has just changed — she has had an idea. Her eyes are wide. Don Aurelio watches her with a small amused smile. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: Renata was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "Can I hear one of them." Don Aurelio was surprised. But he nodded. He took one of the four down — the one that had belonged to Bernardo Molina — and he handed her a bow. "Play something you know," he said. "Anything. So you hear how it sounds in your own hands." Renata put the violin under her chin. She was very careful. She was afraid to move too much. She played the first few bars of a piece she had been working on — a small piece by Bach.

The sound was — she had no words for it. Her school violin was a decent instrument. She had thought it sounded fine. This did not sound fine. This sounded like a completely different thing. It sounded like the note was already alive before she played it. It sounded warm. Golden. Full. She stopped after only a few notes because she was almost afraid to keep going. She handed the violin back to Don Aurelio very carefully. Don Aurelio said, "Yes. That is what a Constanzi sounds like. Now if you hear that sound coming from a violin you did not expect it from — that is the fifth. That is how you would know."

Renata went home that evening on the subway with her school violin in its case, and she thought about the fifth violin the whole way. Somewhere in the world, someone was playing it. Maybe as an ordinary violin. Maybe not even a violin anymore — maybe it was in an attic, or a museum in a small town, or a private collection where nobody had told anyone about it. Two hundred years. It could be anywhere. It could be in Buenos Aires. It could be in her neighborhood.

That night she could not sleep. She had a strange feeling. She got out her school notebook and she started writing things down. What she knew about the violin. What it looked like. What the mark inside said. Where it had last been seen — a merchant's shop in Naples in 1801. Where it might have gone. Ships from Naples went all over the world. Some of them came to Buenos Aires. Many did. In the 1800s. There had been a huge wave of Italian immigration to Argentina. Whole families had come, bringing their belongings, their furniture, their instruments. What if the fifth Constanzi had come to Argentina and had been in the same country the whole time?

paragraphs: On Friday she went back to pick up her violin. She brought her notebook. She said, when she paid for the repair — Don Aurelio waved off the money, as her teacher had said he would — she said, "Don Aurelio. Can I tell you something. I want to help you find the fifth violin." He looked at her for a long moment. He did not laugh. He said, "Renata. My father looked for thirty years. He was a professional. He knew everyone in the field. He never found it. It is not — this is not a project for one afternoon. Or for a schoolgirl."

"I know," said Renata. "But — I want to try. Because — because I heard how it sounds. And I do not want to be a person who does not try to find something like that. Even if it takes me my whole life." Don Aurelio was silent. Then he said, softly, "Very well. If you are serious. I will tell you everything I know. Sit down. Take out your notebook." And he began to talk. He talked for an hour. About what his father had tried. About which routes ships had taken from Naples in the early 1800s. About Italian immigrants in Argentina and what they had brought with them. About specific old families in Buenos Aires who had been musical. Renata wrote it all down.

paragraphs: For the next few years, whenever Renata had free time — after school, on weekends — she worked on the fifth violin. It became her thing. Nobody at her school knew. She did not tell her friends. It was a project she did alone, with occasional visits to Don Aurelio to report and ask questions. She spent hours in old libraries reading passenger records from Italian ships. She visited old cemeteries in Buenos Aires to look at the names of Italian immigrant families who had been buried in the 1800s. She wrote letters to small historical societies. Most of the letters were not answered. Some were answered politely with no useful information. A very few were answered helpfully.

By the time she was fourteen, she had a list of maybe forty families in Buenos Aires who had come from Naples in the early 1800s and who had been at least somewhat musical. She was working on finding descendants of those families. It was slow. It was not something she could push. She had school. She had violin lessons. She had normal life. But she kept the notebook. Every time she found a small new thing, she wrote it in the notebook.

She did not find the violin when she was fourteen. Or fifteen. Or sixteen. When she was seventeen and applying to music schools, she was almost accepted at a conservatory in Milan. She thought about going. But she chose to stay in Buenos Aires because — she realized — she did not want to leave the search. She had been at it for six years by then. She was not going to abandon it. She studied violin at a university in Buenos Aires. She visited Don Aurelio often. Don Aurelio was getting older. His hands were slower now. He still worked, though, and he still kept the four violins on the wall.

The fifth violin found her, not the other way around. She was twenty-three years old. She had just finished her degree. She was giving a small concert at a community center in a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Buenos Aires — a program of folk-tinged classical pieces, meant for people who did not usually go to concerts. She played her violin. Halfway through the program, she noticed an old man in the back. He was very old. He was watching her closely. When the concert was over, he came up to her. He asked if he could speak with her privately.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior scene in a community center hall after a concert. A very old man (Signor Petrini, ninety) speaks with Renata (23, dark hair, formal concert clothes). He is small and wrinkled and dressed in an old-fashioned dark suit. Between them, on a chair, is a very old leather violin case. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: His name was Signor Petrini. He was ninety years old. His grandfather had come from Naples in 1859 and had brought with him a violin that had been in the family since the 1830s. The family had been musical. His grandfather had played it. His father had played it. He himself had played it, until his hands got too shaky, twenty years ago. Now it sat in its case in his apartment. He had no children. He was going to die soon. He was worried about what would happen to it. He had heard Renata play at his neighbor's community center. He had thought — she plays with love. She should have it. If she wanted it.

He opened the case. Inside was a violin. It was old. It was dark amber varnished. It had a curled scroll. Renata's heart was beating in her ears. She lifted the violin very slowly out of its case. She turned it over. She looked inside. Through the f-hole she could see — she could see the label. And on the label was a small careful C inside a small circle. Painted in slightly faded ink. Two hundred and twenty-six years ago.

Don Aurelio (now in his seventies, hair fully silver) has stopped his work and is looking at her, his face very still. On the wall behind him: the four violins as before. Warm afternoon light. paragraphs: She took it to Don Aurelio the next day. She walked up the narrow stairs to the third floor with the old case in her hands, and she opened the door of the workshop without knocking, and Don Aurelio was at the bench, and he looked up. He saw her face first. Then he saw the case. He set down his tools very slowly. He came around the bench. He did not say anything.

Renata put the case on the small customer chair. She opened it. She lifted out the violin. She handed it to Don Aurelio. Don Aurelio took it in both hands. He was very careful with it. He held it up to the light. He turned it slowly. He looked at the fingerboard. He looked at the curl of the scroll. He looked at the back — the wood grain. He looked at the label through the f-hole. He was completely silent for maybe two minutes. Then, very softly, he said, "Oh. Oh. Oh, my father. Oh, my father, look what she found." And he sat down in the customer chair with the violin in his lap, and he cried.

pages.imagePrompt: Mike Mignola style for children: interior close view of the workshop wall. Now five identical violins hang in a row on the wall, all with warm amber varnish and matching scrolls. Renata (23) and Don Aurelio (seventies, silver hair) stand together looking at them. Both are smiling softly. Warm afternoon light. Heavy ink outlines, flat shadows, cream and sepia palette.
paragraphs: They hung it on the wall together, that afternoon. Don Aurelio had had a fifth hook up there for as long as Renata had known him. She had not really noticed it — she had thought it was just an empty hook, waiting for something else. But it had been waiting for this. She helped him lift the fifth violin onto it. Now there were five in a row. All the same. All finally together. Two hundred and twenty-six years after they had left Constanzi's workshop, they were together again.

They stood looking at them for a long time. Don Aurelio said, quietly, "Renata. You know that Signor Petrini — the man who gave it to you — did not know. He did not know what it was. He was giving you a family violin. He did not know he was giving you a Constanzi." Renata said, "I did not tell him. I could not tell him. It felt wrong. He gave it to me because he loved me playing. If I had told him what it was worth, he would have — I don't know. He would have felt differently. He gave it as a gift. I want to take it as a gift." Don Aurelio nodded slowly. "That is the right answer," he said.

Renata played the fifth Constanzi for the rest of her life. She did not sell it. She did not put it in a museum. She played it. She had it insured and she took it to Don Aurelio for a check every year, but otherwise she played it — at concerts, at rehearsals, in her own living room in the afternoons. When she was old, she brought a young student to Don Aurelio's workshop — Don Aurelio had died by then, but his daughter had taken over — and she showed the student the wall of five violins. She said, quietly, "There are four here. Not five. Because one is in my case. And when I die, it will come back and it will hang here with the others. That is the plan. But for now — for now, it is being played."

The young student looked at the four on the wall. She said, "Was there ever a sixth. A Constanzi sextet." Renata smiled. She said, "I do not know. Nobody knows. If there was, it is still lost." The young student nodded seriously. She said, "Then I am going to try to find it." And Renata put her hand on the girl's shoulder, and she said, "Good."
